title: P0 stream choreography deadlock postmortem
summary: On 2029-10-19 we experienced a P0-level degradation for the Hosted API streaming surface: a progressive rise in streaming tail latency and a set of correlated 5xx errors for ~47 minutes. Root cause: a deadlock between the new edge multiplexer release (v6.3.0) and the scheduler backpressure/hysteresis layer that allowed prefetch windows to stall under particular ack-order interleavings. The deadlock prevented stream progress on a subset of long-lived sessions leading to retransmits, increased queueing, and eventual circuit-open behaviour in the egress path.
impact: Affected customers: ~1.8% of active streaming sessions experienced stalls or 5xx fragments; our p95/p99 streaming tail latency spiked ~4-6x; several high-volume tenants reported elevated client reconnect rates and degraded UX across chat and real-time assistant flows. No data loss or model corruption observed. Total incident duration: ~47 minutes (detection to primary mitigation), with follow-up mitigations and mitigations hardening over next 24 hours.
timeline:
2029-10-19 09:12 UTC — New multiplexer v6.3.0 rollout (canary -> 20% -> 60%).
2029-10-19 09:37 UTC — First automated alert: p99 streaming tail latency > 900ms (baseline ~170ms). Pager to SRE on-call fired.
2029-10-19 09:39 UTC — On-call confirms spike, begins query of dashboard traces and streaming ingress/egress rates.
2029-10-19 09:43 UTC — Concurrent increase in streaming fragment 5xx errors observed; traffic skewed to canary hosts.
2029-10-19 09:48 UTC — Hypothesis formed: recent mux change related to ack scheduling. Scoped to multiplexer pods in region-us-west-2.
2029-10-19 09:50 UTC — Temporary mitigation: throttle canary -> rollback trigger prepared.
2029-10-19 09:52 UTC — Emergency rollback of multiplexer to v6.2.7 (completed by 09:58 UTC).
2029-10-19 10:00 UTC — Streaming latency and 5xx rates begin to normalize; indicators back to baseline by 10:07 UTC.
2029-10-20 14:15 UTC — Root cause repro verified in staging with stress harness and long-lived session workload (see linked PR and repro notes).
detection_and_response: Detection: automated telemetry on streaming tail latency plus 5xx fragment alerts. The anomaly surfaced via our p99 tail SLO monitor. Response: on-call executed standard triage (scope, severity, blast radius), identified strong correlation with v6.3.0 hosts using host tags and deployment timestamps, and executed a rollback to v6.2.7. Communication: incident channel created in #sre-incident with product and platform leads looped in; status page updated at 09:58 UTC. Post-rollback monitoring validated recovery before declaring primary mitigation complete.
root_cause: A change in v6.3.0 multiplexer altered the ordering of ack handling for multiplexed client streams. Under normal traffic the change improved throughput, but when combined with a scheduler backpressure hysteresis window optimization (deployed earlier in the quarter), certain sequences of interleaved acks + prefetch window refills could enter a livelock where both multiplexer and scheduler waited for each other’s signals to proceed. This was a logical deadlock (not strictly a mutex), triggered by: (1) long-lived sessions with interleaved small fragments, (2) prefetch window sizes at the lower bound for cost optimization, (3) the interleaving introduced by a new ack coalescing heuristic in v6.3.0.
contributing_factors:
1) Insufficient cross-team rollout coordination — the multiplexer change and scheduler hysteresis change were not tested together in an integrated stress scenario.
2) Canary coverage gap — canary set did not include longer-lived session patterns that reproduce the failure mode.
3) Observability blind spot — our current streaming trace heuristics aggregated ack events away from the timeline that mattered (we collapsed acks in telemetry), making root-cause linking slower.
4) Runbook gap — no explicit runbook action to prioritize rolling back multiplexer vs. increasing prefetch window; team defaulted to rollback, which was effective but caused some manual hesitancy initially.
short_term_mitigation: Immediate rollback of multiplexer v6.3.0 to v6.2.7 across affected regions. Temporarily increase prefetch window lower bound in the scheduler for long-lived sessions while we further harden validation tests. Re-opened canary gating to require long-session traffic in future canaries.
long_term_mitigation:
1) Patch multiplexer v6.3.0: restore deterministic ack-ordering and introduce a watchdog that breaks cycles if no progress after 250ms. PR #872 contains a fix and regression tests.
2) Update scheduler to include liveness interrupts for prefetch waiting so it can't wait indefinitely for an ack that was coalesced.
3) Add an integrated stress test to our CI that runs longer-lived interleaved fragment patterns (10–20 minute sessions) against combinations of multiplexer and scheduler versions.
4) Enforce cross-team rollout sign-off for any change touching streaming ack/flow-control semantics.
runbook_changes:
1) Add a specific checklist step for 'identify last multiplexer version change' when streaming tail latency > threshold.
2) Add explicit decision tree: if streaming 5xx + tail latency correlate to a recent mux rollout, prefer rollback as first mitigation unless deployment window is constrained.
3) Add runbook procedure for 'increase scheduler prefetch lower bound' with exact flags and impact notes.
4) Add observability recipe: do not collapse acks in p99 streaming timeline traces; surface ack interleaving counts.

Attached logs: mux trace showing ack coalescer suppressed individual ack events (mux-log-1312), scheduler trace showing prefetch wait state (sched-log-2407).
